reply.title: At the Highest Point of a Vertical Throw
reply.story:
When you toss a ball straight up into the air, it slows down as it climbs, hangs motionless for a fraction of a second at its highest point, and then speeds up as it falls back down. Watching it pause at the top, it is tempting to think that since its speed is zero, its acceleration must also be zero at that exact moment.

Yet if acceleration were zero at the peak, the ball would stay there suspended in mid-air rather than turning around. To see why the ball keeps changing its motion, we can look at the constant pull of gravity acting on it throughout the flight. Even when the velocity is momentarily zero, gravity continues to pull downward with a steady force.

By tracking both the velocity and the acceleration side by side on a timeline and a graph, we can separate how fast the ball is moving from how fast its velocity is changing. The slope of the velocity curve remains steady the entire time, proving that gravity never stops working even at the very top.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how a ball's velocity and acceleration behave during a vertical throw. Even when the velocity is $0\text{ m/s}$ at the apex, the downward acceleration remains constant at $-g$.
reply.instructions: Adjust the launch speed and gravity, then press play to observe the motion and the velocity-time plot.
